title: Structural and mechanistic insights into azetidine-associated αKG-NHFe enzyme OkaE with multifunctional catalysis

paper_content.introduction:
α-Ketoglutarate-dependentmononuclearnon-haemiron(αKG-NHFe)enzymesplaycrucialrolesinnaturalproductbiosynthesisthroughareactiveFeIV=Ospecies to selectively abstract hydrogen atom from substrate C–H bonds via a Hydrogen Atom Transfer (HAT), driving oxidations that generate structurally diverse and biologically significantnaturalproducts1,2.Thisenzymefamilyexhibitscatalyticversatility,including hydroxylation, ring fragmentation, C–C bond cleavage,epimerization,desaturation,endoperoxidation,andheterocycleformation3.While~70%ofreportedαKG-NHFeenzymescatalyseasingletypeofreaction1,3,4,theremaining30%enzymesexhibitmultifunctionality, contributing to diverse biological processes such as cellular metabolism, signaling, and biosynthesis of complex natural products1.ProminentexamplesofmultifunctionalαKG-NHFeenzymesinclude FtmOx15–9, AsqJ10, VioC11, SptF12, DnmT13, AusE14, PrhA14, DAOCS15, HppD16, EFE17, AndA18, and DabC19. These multifunctional enzymes exhibit catalytic versatility, often facilitating complex chemicaltransformationsthatyieldstructurallydiverseandbiologicallyactivemetabolites20,21.

Structural classification based on αKG coordination geometry reveals two distinct modes, distal-type and proximal-type, each accountingfor~50%ofknownαKG-NHFeenzymes1.Theproximal-typeenzymespositionthecatalyticferrylspeciesadjacenttothesubstratefordirectoxygeninsertiontypicalofsimplehydroxylation.However,indistal-typeenzymes,αKGcoordinatesinsuchawaythattheFeIV=Ospeciesispositionedawayfromthesubstrate,promotingmorecomplicatedreactionsviaemergingmechanisticmodelsinvolvingaminoacid radical-mediated process in the COX-like model of FtmOx1-catalysis5,7,αKGrotationinAsqJ-catalysis10,andFeIV=Ospeciesrotationin WelO5- and SyrB2-catalysis22,23. Notably, in distal-type αKG-NHFeenzymes, both substrate activation and access to multiple reactive sites are critical for enabling multifunctional catalysis, as demonstrated in AusE14, PrhA14, and SptF12. A deeper understanding of the catalytic mechanisms on these distal-type enzymes is crucial for advancing enzyme engineering,biocatalysis,anddrugdiscovery.

Theazetidinescaffoldisafour-memberedsaturatedcyclicamine(Fig.1a),andisfoundinrelativelyfewnaturalproductswithdistinctivephysiological functionalities24. Notable examples include quorum-sensing regulation azetidomonamides25, antifungal and anticancer vioprolides26, anti-Alzheimer’s disease candidate bonnevillamides27, insecticidal okaramines28, and anti-fungal polyoxins29. Beyond their natural occurrence, azetidines are increasingly valued as important pharmacophores in medicinalchemistry30, offering enhanced three-dimensionality31, favorable pharmacokinetic properties32,33, and reducedlipophilicity34,therebyaddressingcriticalchallengesindrugdesign. However, chemical synthesis of the azetidine ring remains particularlychallengingduetotheirhighstrainandintrinsicinstabilityrelativetofive-orsix-memberedN-heterocycles(Fig.1a).Conventionalsyntheticroutesofteninvolvedstrainedtransitionstates,high-energyintermediates, and multistep sequences to overcome significant kineticandentropicbarriers35,36.

In contrast,naturehasevolved specialized enzymes capable of assemblingthisstrainedringwithefficiencyandselectivity.Todate,only five biosynthetically validated azetidine-ring forming enzymes havebeenreported36,37.MostoperatethroughS-adenosylmethionine(SAM)-dependent intramolecular cyclization, including Class I methyltransferasesVioH38,NAS39,andAzeJ25,whichcatalyzeintramolecular C–N bond formation with concomitant release of 5′-methylthioadenosine (MTA)36. A mechanistically distinct case is the haem-oxygenase-likediironoxidasePolF,whichmediatesC–Ncyclizationinthebiosynthesisofpolyoxamicacid37(Fig.1b).

Strikinglydivergentfromthisparadigm,thebiosyntheticpathwayof okaramines, a class of complex indole alkaloids isolated from PenicilliumandAspergillusspecies28,involvesanαKG-NHFeenzyme,OkaE,capableofcatalyzingazetidineringformationviaC–Cformation(Fig.1c).Notably,OkaEistheonlycharacterizedmemberoftheαKG-NHFefamilycapableofmediatingthisunusualcyclization,positioningitasabiochemicalanomalywithsignificantmechanisticandpharmacophoreimplications40,41.Beyondazetidineringformation,OkaEalsofacilitatessubsequenthydroxylation,demonstratingmultifunctionality. However, despite Lin and co-workers’ elucidation of OkaE’s dual catalytic role42, key questions remain unresolved, particularlyconcerningthemechanismoftheFeIV=OmediatedazetidineringformationanditsdivergencefromclassicalαKG-NHFeoxidativechemistry.Inaddition,okaraminesexhibitpotentinsecticidalactivitybyselectivelyactivatingglutamate-gatedchloridechannels(GluCls)ininvertebrates,withoutaffectinghumanligand-gatedanionchannels43.Thisselectivitymakesokaraminespromisingleadsforinsecticidalpharmacophoredesign.GiventhedualfunctionalityofOkaEandtheunresolvedmechanisticquestionssurroundingitsreactivity,adeeperinvestigationofits catalytic mechanism and subsequent protein engineeringholdssignificantpotentialforadvancingbiocatalyticandinsecticidedesign.

Inthisstudy,wecharacterizedOkaEinvitroanduncovereditsmultifunctionalityandcatalyticpromiscuity.Inadditiontoazetidineringformationandhydroxylation,OkaEwasfoundtocatalyzeaseriesof oxidation reactions on the substrate okaramine A (1), including carboxylation, epoxidation, ring fragmentation, and alcohol dehydrogenation (Fig. 2b). Through an integrative approach combining isotopic labelling, X-ray crystallography, quantum mechanics/molecularmechanics(QM/MM)calculations,andproteinengineering,we decipheredthemechanistichierarchygoverningthismultifunctionalcatalysis.Keyinsightsincludedthefollowing:(i)theidentificationofconformationalchangesintheFeIV=OspeciesofOkaE;(ii)thedetermination of distinct hydrogen abstraction sites on the substrate, enablingbifurcatedreactionpathways;(iii)thecharacterizationofareactioninvolvingaseconddioxygenmolecule,asseeninendoperoxidaseslikeFtmOx1andNvfI;and(iv)elucidationofamethionine–π(Met–π)interactionnetworkthatmodulatessubstratepositioningandradical propagation. These insights, spanning atomic to molecular levels, established a unified framework explaining the multifunctionalityand catalytic plasticityofOkaE.Bymappingstructure-functionrelationshipsacrossmultiplecatalyticmodalities,thisworkprovides a blueprint for engineering next-generation biocatalysts capableoforchestratingcomplexsynthetictransformations.

In the OkaE mutant, enzymatic reaction preference was restrictedtotheC8apositionduetoextensiverearrangementoftheMet–πnetwork.RemovaloftheindolylgroupofW79disruptedtheinteractionsbetweenM64andindoletailof1,causingan~120°rotationoftheM64sidechainalongitsCα –CβbondandtheformationofanewstackinginteractionwithA79andtheindoletailof1(Fig.5c).AnewhydrogenbondwasformedbetweensulfuratomofM64andthehydroxylgroupatC3a(Fig.5c).Thesechangesinducedan~3.4°bendoftheindoletailof1towardtheC−Gringsplaneandan~11.4°rotationoftheD−Eringstowardmetallo-centre(Fig.5d,g).Takentogether,these conformational shifts increased the distance between the metallo-centreandO3afrom5.7Åto6.4Å,whilethedistancebetweenthe metallo-centre and the C8a remained unchanged compared to OkaE ,preventingO3ahydrogenabstractionandenforcingC8aasthesolereactive site (Fig. 5d, g). For compounds 3−6, although the catalytic cycle of αKG-NHFeenzymeswasactivatedbyO ,theoxygenatominFeIII−OHandFeIV=Ospeciescanbeexchangedwithsolventwater50,51duringcatalysis. Alternatively, oxygen incorporation may occur via transient cationic intermediates49,51involvingwatermolecules.Forcompound7,biochemicalassaysrevealedthatitsyieldremainedunchangedwhen themolarratioofαKG:1wasincreasedfrom1:1to4:1(Fig.2b),suggestingthat7arisesfromasingleαKG-dependentcatalyticreactionratherthanfrommultipleroundsofoxidativecatalysis.Intraceivof7(Fig.6e),the+2peakwasnearlyundetectable,whereasthe+0and+4peaksappearedinalmostequalproportions(m/z551(+0):553(+2):555(+4)=46.7%:1.3%:52.0%),furthersupportingtheinvolvementofa second dioxygenmolecule withina single reactioncycle. Based on structure-function analyses, QM/MM calculations, and isotope-labellingexperiments,weproposedacatalyticmechanismfortheconsecutiveoxidationreactionscatalysedbyOkaE,asdepictedinFig.7andSupplementaryFigs.26–30.TherapidadditionofO tothemetallo-centre generates the FeIV=O species. The formation of neuokaramine IV (7) (Fig. 7c) begins with hydrogenabstractionattheO3apositionof1(purplearrow,pathb), formingFeIII−OHandasubstrateradicalIMd.TheradicalthentransferstoC8a,generatingintermediateIMd ,whichleadstotheformationofacarbonylgroupatC3aandcleavageoftheC3a−C8abond.Before hydroxyl rebound at C8a with the FeIII−OH species, the C8a−radicalreactswithO toformaperoxylradicalIMd .Theresultingperoxyl radical attacks C11 to form an endoperoxide-containing intermediate IMd . Subsequently, FeIII−OH abstracts the hydrogen atom at C8a, leading to cleavage of the endoperoxide bridge and formationofanamido-carbonylgroupatC8a,alongsideanepoxide ring connecting C11 and C12, thereby yielding 7. reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript reports the structural and mechanistic insights into the α-ketoglutarate (αKG)-dependent non-heme iron
enzyme OkaE that builds the azetidine ring in okaramine biosynthesis. In vitro reconstitution of OkaE with okaramine A (1)
produced okaramine E (3), 12-dehydroxy-okaramine E (2), and four new congeners, neokaramines I–IV (4–7). Crystal
structures of OkaE•Co²⁺, OkaE•Co²⁺•αKG, and OkaE•Co²⁺•αKG•okaramine A revealed a homodimeric double-stranded β-
helix fold, a distal-type αKG binding mode, and placement of substrate atoms C8a and O3a near the metal center within a
pocket framed by M64, M71, M122, and W79. QM/MM calculations supported the distal αKG geometry and showed substrate
positioning that shortens Op–H8a and Op–H3a distances (≈4.8→2.9 Å and 5.1→2.6 Å). Site-directed mutagenesis indicated
that M71A biases H8a hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT), W79A reduces overall reactivity, and M122A modestly enhances
formation of 7 via O3a-HAT; structures of M64A, M71A, and W79A complexes corroborate these product profiles. Isotope-
18O-labeling showed mixed O₂/H₂O incorporation into 3–6, consistent with hydroxyl-rebound and/or cationic pathways,
whereas 7 incorporates only O₂, implying rare capture of a second O₂ within a single catalytic cycle. Together, the data
support a mechanism in which H8a-HAT drives azetidine formation followed by sequential
oxidations to give 2–6, while a possible alternate O3a-HAT pathway channels
peroxidation/epoxidation to yield 7. Overall, the study elucidates the structure-function relationships of OkaE and demonstrates its potential to be reprogrammed to tailor and
diversify complex natural products. Specific comments are listed as follows,
1. Figure 4. In vitro assays showed that M64A converts substrate 1 to 7, whereas M71A did not (Figure 4A,B). The proposed
pathway for 7 formation involves abstraction of the C3a–OH proton. However, the crystal structures place the C3a–OH at the
same distance from the metal center in both M64A and M71A (~5.9 Å). How do the authors explain these divergent
outcomes with the similar C3a–OH–metal distances?
2. Page 5, Line 117, the authors mentioned “four previously uncharacterized minor products, designated as neuokaramines
I–IV (4–7),” but on Page 6, Lines 140–141 stated that “the structure of 6 was identical to that of okaramine R.” In reference
43, the stereochemistry at C-3a of okaramine R was not determined in reference 43, while the present study showed the
configuration of C-3a OH on the structure (Scheme 1). Please provide how to verify the stereochemistry of C-3a OH of
compound 6 or if it could be okaramine R reported in reference 43.
3. For structure elucidation of the enzymatic products, please provide detailed stereochemical descriptions of compounds 4–
7, especially for protons like H-2, H-12, and H-11. Please explain how the stereochemistry of compounds 4–7 based on
NOESY or other spectroscopic data.
4. Is there any evidence to support that IM2 is involved in the conversion of 3 to 4 or 5?
5. Figure 4, the in vitro experiment of M71A with 1 showed several additional signals compared to those in WT with 1 (e.g.
retention time around 14 min and 33 min). Did the authors have any idea what the products may be and if they are related to
okaramines?
6. For Figure 5, please provide the corresponding mass spectra in SI.
7. Page 11 to 12, the contents described the structure rearrangement of OkaE•CoII and OkaE•CoII•αKG•okaramine A (1)
complex (for example, the conformational shift of the beta-helix formed by I269-S270 ). It is suggested to add Figures in the
main text or SI to show the comparison and structure superimposition figure of OkaE•CoII and OkaE•CoII•αKG•okaramine A
(1) complex.
8. Page 30, line 595, “Table S8” should be “Table S7”.
9. Please check the stereochemistry of C-2 of the structures shown in Figure 1. Some structures did not show the
stereochemistry properly.
10. In the Experimental section, please clearly specify which procedures were performed under aerobic versus anaerobic
conditions.
Supporting Information:
1. Figure S11: The current legend for Figure S11 mentioned “Peak 1” (void) and “Peak 2” (OkaE), but these peaks are not
labeled or indicated in the figure. Please revise the legend to match the actual presentation of the chromatogram.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript describes the multifunctionality of OkaE, an αKG-dependent non-haem iron enzyme, in azetidine formation
and subsequent scaffold diversification. While the authors report in vitro assays, crystallography, and QM/MM simulations,
the study lacks novelty since the catalytic versatility of this enzyme family is well documented, and the presented findings do
not substantially advance mechanistic understanding. Furthermore, the work is not thorough: the mechanistic evidence is
insufficiently supported, the structural interpretations are speculative. Overall, the manuscript does not reach the standard of
originality or rigor required for publication.
Comments:
Line 120: Regarding the observed differenced from Lin et al. results, differences in reaction conditions should be clearly
described in the main text.
Line 127: I believe it is unlikely that only one eq. of aKG is needed for 4, 5, 7.
Line 152: The biochemical evidence should be clearly presented.
Fig4a: The authors assume that 3,4,5,6 are generated through H8b-HAT, and 7 is formed via OH3a-HAT. However, no
experimental evidence is provided to correlate the site of HAT with the product structures.
Fig 6a: Formation of a primary cation Ima3 should be less likely.
Fig 6c: The mechanism shown in 6c involving second O2 is not fully supported by the results. What would happen if the
authors use a mixture of 16O2 and 18O2? Product with 16O/18O should be formed if the hypothesis is correct.
1. The QM/MM calculations mainly address the formation of the Fe(IV)=O species; additional simulations on the later stages
of the reaction would provide deeper mechanistic understanding.
2. For compound 7, determining the oxygen stoichiometry would provide more solid evidence supporting the proposed
involvement of two dioxygen molecules in a single catalytic cycle.
3. In the 18O-labeling experiments, using a mixture of 18O2 and 16O2 could provide critical insights into the incorporation of
two oxygen atoms during the formation of 7.
4. The map levels should be indicated in the legends of Supplementary Figures S13 and S16.
5. In Figure 2, the meaning of the black dashed lines in panels d and f should also be clarified in the legend.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
“Structural and Mechanistic Insights into Azetidine-associated αKG NHFe Enzyme OkaE with Multifunctional Catalysis” by
Wang, Yu, Liu, Zhang, Zhu, Yan, and Liu et al. is about OkaE, a α-Ketoglutarate-dependent mononuclear non-haem iron
enzyme that can synthesize a pharmacophoric motif azetidine ring via unique C–C bond formation. The authors find that
OkaE also performs sequential oxidations such as hydroxylations, epoxidation, and ring cleavages. The authors find that not
one but two oxygen molecules are involved for sequential epoxidation and ring cleavage. The authors use a host of
experimental techniques (isotopic labeling, X-ray crystallography, and protein engineering), along with QM/MM calculations
to understand the reactivity of OkaE.
Although this article is well written and sound, I have a few concerns that should be addressed prior to publication of the
article. I commend the authors on a comprehensive work with the methods being described in a very reproducible way. I
urge the authors to consider my suggestions below and upload their simulation data so that it can be reused by the
community..
1. The authors mention that OkaE undergoes HAT. Are the authors sure about this, or do they mean Proton-Coupled
Electron Transfer (PCET) in the general sense? https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/anie.201805511. Here, HAT
may imply a mechanistic picture that the authors are not fully implying. There should be a clarification on this point.
2. How did the authors choose their E-value threshold for the sequence similarity analysis? Is this just a strict cutoff that finds
the most similar sequences? If so, why not a multiple sequence alignment?
3. The authors mention that the substrate binding pocket size is reduced by 10% when they analyze their structures. Is this a
fair analysis? Static structures may not indicate the true reduction in the effective pocket size which may be influenced by the
dynamics. Is the spread of this pocket size minimal? The authors may have an answer from their QM/MM simulations.
4. There are some typos that should be fixed. Page 12 line 227, “coplaner”. Page 18 line 329: ‘to addressing this’
5. In figure 4b, why do the bars not all add up to 100%? At a minimum, shouldn’t the wild type bars add up to 100%?
6. The isotope labeling experiments in this work are beautiful. However, I do not follow why the alphaKG ratio being altered
to 4:1 indicates the involvement of the second dioxygen. This should be explained in a bit more detail for readers. The
speciation of the second oxygen must be different if it is what the readers indicate. What is the form of this hypothesized
second oxygen species likely to be?
7. When altering between axial and equatorial conformations for the iron oxo, there may be a transition state:
https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acscatal.2c01143. How would OkaE overcome such a barrier in the proposed
mechanism? Some commentary on this would be helpful.
8. I urge the authors to upload their data to zenodo instead of making their data available upon request. This will facilitate the
reuse of the authors’ work.
The article is well written. Thus, I’d like to commend the authors on this effort.

catalytic versatility, we believe our work on OkaE provides several new insights that

(1) Regarding novelty issue on “…the study lacks novelty since the catalytic
versatility of this enzyme family is well documented, and the presented findings do
not substantially advance mechanistic understanding…”:
We apologize for the insufficient emphasis on these aspects in the original
manuscript. Our study on OkaE presents several key advances, as summarized below:
i) OkaE represents a new paradigm in enzymatic scaffold diversification. Unlike
previously reported systems by Lin group3, OkaE enzyme is a single enzyme
capable that catalyzes multiple distinct chemical steps, including hydroxylation,
cyclization, and possibly rearrangement, to assemble and diversify a complex
azetidine-containing scaffold. This function versatility provides a new biosynthetic
model for scaffold diversification in natural product biosynthesis.
ii) First atomic-resolution view of azetidine formation. By integrating of
crystallography with QM/MM simulations, we provide the first atomic-level
insight into azetidine ring formation within this enzyme family, addressing a novel
and unresolved mechanistic question.
iii) Discovery of a potential new peroxygenase-like activity in non-heme iron
enzyme. Our isotopic labeling experiments reveal that OkaE incorporates an
oxygen molecule to form an endoperoxide during catalysis. This function trait,
observed in only a few αKG-dependent non-haem iron enzyme such as FtmOx17-
15
11and NvfI12, suggests that OkaE may represent a third functionally distinct system
capable of endoperoxide formation. This finding not only expands the mechanistic
repertoire of this enzyme family but also highlights OkaE as a promising starting
point for engineering novel biocatalysts that exploit peroxide-bridge intermediates
for selective C‒H bond activation.
iv) The Met–π interaction network controls pathway bifurcation and offers a new
engineering principle. The structure of OkaE in complex with okaramine A
reveals a unique the Met–π interaction network (M64-M71-W79-M122) that envelops
the A-ring of the substrate. Site-directed mutagenesis demonstrates that this
network is critical structural determinant of reaction bifurcation: the M71A variant
shifts selectivity toward the H8a–HAT pathway, yielding predominantly 6,
whereas W79A disrupts bifurcation entirely. This provides decisive experimental
evidence that Met–π network is not merely structural but functionally essential.
Furthermore, this study offers the first example of leveraging a Met–π interaction
network to engineer catalytic pathway bifurcation for natural product
diversification.
v) A distal αKG-binding mode enables novel oxygen activation. The OkaE enzyme
and substrate complex exhibits a distal-type αKG-binding mode that prevents
conventional rebound hydroxylation. QM/MM calculations support a feasible
azetidine-formation pathway and reveal that rotation of the FeIV=O species initiates
two competing HAT channels (3a-OH–HAT and H8a–HAT), rationalizing the
product diversity. This study expands the repertoire of distal-type αKG enzymes
and provides quantitative computational validation of their potential for non-
canonical oxygen activation mechanisms, offering new prospects for predicting
and engineering novel enzyme functions.

Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. OkaE follows the classical
catalytic paradigm of αKG-dependent non-heme iron enzymes, in which the high-spin
(S = 2) FeIV=O intermediate cleaves substrate C–H bonds via a Hydrogen Atom
Transfer (HAT) mechanism13. As noted by the reviewer, the distinction between these

3. How did the authors choose their E-value threshold for the sequence similarity
analysis? Is this just a strict cutoff that finds the most similar sequences? If so, why not
a multiple sequence alignment?
Response:
The E-value threshold was chosen based on established practice in BLAST-based
sequence similarity searches, where increasingly stringent cutoffs are commonly
applied to balance sensitivity and specificity. Specifically, we examined three
thresholds (10−30, 10−50, and 10−70) to ensure that our results were not dependent on a
single value. This approach allowed us to focus on highly similar sequences, thereby
enabling reliable structural comparison and mechanistic interpretation. While multiple
sequence alignment is indeed a powerful complementary method, its primary utility lies
in identifying conserved motifs and residue-level variation across a broader set of
homologs. Our specific aim here was instead to capture the most closely related
homologous sequences to guide structural modeling and functional inference. For this
purpose, E-value–based filtering provides a more direct and appropriate framework.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript reports the structural and mechanistic insights into the α-ketoglutarate (αKG)-dependent non-heme iron
enzyme OkaE that builds the azetidine ring in okaramine biosynthesis. In vitro reconstitution of OkaE with okaramine A (1)
produced okaramine E (3), 12-dehydroxy-okaramine E (2), and four new congeners, neokaramines I–IV (4–7). Crystal
structures of OkaE•Co²⁺, OkaE•Co²⁺•αKG, and OkaE•Co²⁺•αKG•okaramine A revealed a homodimeric double-stranded β-
helix fold, a distal-type αKG binding mode, and placement of substrate atoms C8a and O3a near the metal center within a
pocket framed by M64, M71, M122, and W79. QM/MM calculations supported the distal αKG geometry and showed substrate
positioning that shortens Op–H8a and Op–H3a distances (≈4.8→2.9 Å and 5.1→2.6 Å). Site-directed mutagenesis indicated
that M71A biases H8a hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT), W79A reduces overall reactivity, and M122A modestly enhances
formation of 7 via O3a-HAT; structures of M64A, M71A, and W79A complexes corroborate these product profiles. Isotope-
18O-labeling showed mixed O₂/H₂O incorporation into 3–6, consistent with hydroxyl-rebound and/or cationic pathways,
whereas 7 incorporates only O₂, implying rare capture of a second O₂ within a single catalytic cycle. Together, the data
support a mechanism in which H8a-HAT drives azetidine formation followed by sequential
oxidations to give 2–6, while a possible alternate O3a-HAT pathway channels
peroxidation/epoxidation to yield 7. Overall, the study elucidates the structure-function relationships of OkaE and demonstrates its potential to be reprogrammed to tailor and
diversify complex natural products. Specific comments are listed as follows,
1. Figure 4. In vitro assays showed that M64A converts substrate 1 to 7, whereas M71A did not (Figure 4A,B). The proposed
pathway for 7 formation involves abstraction of the C3a–OH proton. However, the crystal structures place the C3a–OH at the
same distance from the metal center in both M64A and M71A (~5.9 Å). How do the authors explain these divergent
outcomes with the similar C3a–OH–metal distances?
2. Page 5, Line 117, the authors mentioned “four previously uncharacterized minor products, designated as neuokaramines
I–IV (4–7),” but on Page 6, Lines 140–141 stated that “the structure of 6 was identical to that of okaramine R.” In reference
43, the stereochemistry at C-3a of okaramine R was not determined in reference 43, while the present study showed the
configuration of C-3a OH on the structure (Scheme 1). Please provide how to verify the stereochemistry of C-3a OH of
compound 6 or if it could be okaramine R reported in reference 43.
3. For structure elucidation of the enzymatic products, please provide detailed stereochemical descriptions of compounds 4–
7, especially for protons like H-2, H-12, and H-11. Please explain how the stereochemistry of compounds 4–7 based on
NOESY or other spectroscopic data.
4. Is there any evidence to support that IM2 is involved in the conversion of 3 to 4 or 5?
5. Figure 4, the in vitro experiment of M71A with 1 showed several additional signals compared to those in WT with 1 (e.g.
retention time around 14 min and 33 min). Did the authors have any idea what the products may be and if they are related to
okaramines?
6. For Figure 5, please provide the corresponding mass spectra in SI.
7. Page 11 to 12, the contents described the structure rearrangement of OkaE•CoII and OkaE•CoII•αKG•okaramine A (1)
complex (for example, the conformational shift of the beta-helix formed by I269-S270 ). It is suggested to add Figures in the
main text or SI to show the comparison and structure superimposition figure of OkaE•CoII and OkaE•CoII•αKG•okaramine A
(1) complex.
8. Page 30, line 595, “Table S8” should be “Table S7”.
9. Please check the stereochemistry of C-2 of the structures shown in Figure 1. Some structures did not show the
stereochemistry properly.
10. In the Experimental section, please clearly specify which procedures were performed under aerobic versus anaerobic
conditions.
Supporting Information:
1. Figure S11: The current legend for Figure S11 mentioned “Peak 1” (void) and “Peak 2” (OkaE), but these peaks are not
labeled or indicated in the figure. Please revise the legend to match the actual presentation of the chromatogram.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript describes the multifunctionality of OkaE, an αKG-dependent non-haem iron enzyme, in azetidine formation
and subsequent scaffold diversification. While the authors report in vitro assays, crystallography, and QM/MM simulations,
the study lacks novelty since the catalytic versatility of this enzyme family is well documented, and the presented findings do
not substantially advance mechanistic understanding. Furthermore, the work is not thorough: the mechanistic evidence is
insufficiently supported, the structural interpretations are speculative. Overall, the manuscript does not reach the standard of
originality or rigor required for publication.
Comments:
Line 120: Regarding the observed differenced from Lin et al. results, differences in reaction conditions should be clearly
described in the main text.
Line 127: I believe it is unlikely that only one eq. of aKG is needed for 4, 5, 7.
Line 152: The biochemical evidence should be clearly presented.
Fig4a: The authors assume that 3,4,5,6 are generated through H8b-HAT, and 7 is formed via OH3a-HAT. However, no
experimental evidence is provided to correlate the site of HAT with the product structures.
Fig 6a: Formation of a primary cation Ima3 should be less likely.
Fig 6c: The mechanism shown in 6c involving second O2 is not fully supported by the results. What would happen if the
authors use a mixture of 16O2 and 18O2? Product with 16O/18O should be formed if the hypothesis is correct.
1. The QM/MM calculations mainly address the formation of the Fe(IV)=O species; additional simulations on the later stages
of the reaction would provide deeper mechanistic understanding.
2. For compound 7, determining the oxygen stoichiometry would provide more solid evidence supporting the proposed
involvement of two dioxygen molecules in a single catalytic cycle.
3. In the 18O-labeling experiments, using a mixture of 18O2 and 16O2 could provide critical insights into the incorporation of
two oxygen atoms during the formation of 7.
4. The map levels should be indicated in the legends of Supplementary Figures S13 and S16.
5. In Figure 2, the meaning of the black dashed lines in panels d and f should also be clarified in the legend.

### Reviewer 3

“Structural and Mechanistic Insights into Azetidine-associated αKG NHFe Enzyme OkaE with Multifunctional Catalysis” by
Wang, Yu, Liu, Zhang, Zhu, Yan, and Liu et al. is about OkaE, a α-Ketoglutarate-dependent mononuclear non-haem iron
enzyme that can synthesize a pharmacophoric motif azetidine ring via unique C–C bond formation. The authors find that
OkaE also performs sequential oxidations such as hydroxylations, epoxidation, and ring cleavages. The authors find that not
one but two oxygen molecules are involved for sequential epoxidation and ring cleavage. The authors use a host of
experimental techniques (isotopic labeling, X-ray crystallography, and protein engineering), along with QM/MM calculations
to understand the reactivity of OkaE.
Although this article is well written and sound, I have a few concerns that should be addressed prior to publication of the
article. I commend the authors on a comprehensive work with the methods being described in a very reproducible way. I
urge the authors to consider my suggestions below and upload their simulation data so that it can be reused by the
community..
1. The authors mention that OkaE undergoes HAT. Are the authors sure about this, or do they mean Proton-Coupled
Electron Transfer (PCET) in the general sense? https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/anie.201805511. Here, HAT
may imply a mechanistic picture that the authors are not fully implying. There should be a clarification on this point.
2. How did the authors choose their E-value threshold for the sequence similarity analysis? Is this just a strict cutoff that finds
the most similar sequences? If so, why not a multiple sequence alignment?
3. The authors mention that the substrate binding pocket size is reduced by 10% when they analyze their structures. Is this a
fair analysis? Static structures may not indicate the true reduction in the effective pocket size which may be influenced by the
dynamics. Is the spread of this pocket size minimal? The authors may have an answer from their QM/MM simulations.
4. There are some typos that should be fixed. Page 12 line 227, “coplaner”. Page 18 line 329: ‘to addressing this’
5. In figure 4b, why do the bars not all add up to 100%? At a minimum, shouldn’t the wild type bars add up to 100%?
6. The isotope labeling experiments in this work are beautiful. However, I do not follow why the alphaKG ratio being altered
to 4:1 indicates the involvement of the second dioxygen. This should be explained in a bit more detail for readers. The
speciation of the second oxygen must be different if it is what the readers indicate. What is the form of this hypothesized
second oxygen species likely to be?
7. When altering between axial and equatorial conformations for the iron oxo, there may be a transition state:
https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acscatal.2c01143. How would OkaE overcome such a barrier in the proposed
mechanism? Some commentary on this would be helpful.
8. I urge the authors to upload their data to zenodo instead of making their data available upon request. This will facilitate the
reuse of the authors’ work.
The article is well written. Thus, I’d like to commend the authors on this effort.

The manuscript reports the structural and mechanistic insights into the α-ketoglutarate (αKG)-dependent non-heme iron
enzyme OkaE that builds the azetidine ring in okaramine biosynthesis. In vitro reconstitution of OkaE with okaramine A (1)

pocket framed by M64, M71, M122, and W79. QM/MM calculations supported the distal αKG geometry and showed substrate
positioning that shortens Op–H8a and Op–H3a distances (≈4.8→2.9 Å and 5.1→2.6 Å). Site-directed mutagenesis indicated

oxidations to give 2–6, while a possible alternate O3a-HAT pathway channels

“Structural and Mechanistic Insights into Azetidine-associated αKG NHFe Enzyme OkaE with Multifunctional Catalysis” by
Wang, Yu, Liu, Zhang, Zhu, Yan, and Liu et al. is about OkaE, a α-Ketoglutarate-dependent mononuclear non-haem iron
enzyme that can synthesize a pharmacophoric motif azetidine ring via unique C–C bond formation. The authors find that

experimental techniques (isotopic labeling, X-ray crystallography, and protein engineering), along with QM/MM calculations

Although this article is well written and sound, I have a few concerns that should be addressed prior to publication of the
article. I commend the authors on a comprehensive work with the methods being described in a very reproducible way. I
urge the authors to consider my suggestions below and upload their simulation data so that it can be reused by the
community..
1. The authors mention that OkaE undergoes HAT. Are the authors sure about this, or do they mean Proton-Coupled
Electron Transfer (PCET) in the general sense? https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/anie.201805511. Here, HAT

2. How did the authors choose their E-value threshold for the sequence similarity analysis? Is this just a strict cutoff that finds

3. The authors mention that the substrate binding pocket size is reduced by 10% when they analyze their structures. Is this a

relationships of OkaE and demonstrates its potential to be reprogrammed to tailor and

1. The manuscript describes the multifunctionality of OkaE, an αKG-dependent non-

Response:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We have carefully
considered the critiques regarding the novelty and thoroughness of our study. While we
acknowledge that the αKG-dependent non-haem iron enzyme family is known for its
catalytic versatility, we believe our work on OkaE provides several new insights that
substantially advance the field. Below, we address the specific concerns point by point,
and we hope the reviewer will find our response and the additional clarifications in the
revised manuscript persuasive.
(1) Regarding novelty issue on “…the study lacks novelty since the catalytic
versatility of this enzyme family is well documented, and the presented findings do
not substantially advance mechanistic understanding…”:
We apologize for the insufficient emphasis on these aspects in the original
manuscript. Our study on OkaE presents several key advances, as summarized below:
i) OkaE represents a new paradigm in enzymatic scaffold diversification. Unlike
previously reported systems by Lin group3, OkaE enzyme is a single enzyme
capable that catalyzes multiple distinct chemical steps, including hydroxylation,
cyclization, and possibly rearrangement, to assemble and diversify a complex
azetidine-containing scaffold. This function versatility provides a new biosynthetic
model for scaffold diversification in natural product biosynthesis.
ii) First atomic-resolution view of azetidine formation. By integrating of
crystallography with QM/MM simulations, we provide the first atomic-level
insight into azetidine ring formation within this enzyme family, addressing a novel
and unresolved mechanistic question.
iii) Discovery of a potential new peroxygenase-like activity in non-heme iron
enzyme. Our isotopic labeling experiments reveal that OkaE incorporates an
oxygen molecule to form an endoperoxide during catalysis. This function trait,
observed in only a few αKG-dependent non-haem iron enzyme such as FtmOx17-
15
11and NvfI12, suggests that OkaE may represent a third functionally distinct system
capable of endoperoxide formation. This finding not only expands the mechanistic
repertoire of this enzyme family but also highlights OkaE as a promising starting
point for engineering novel biocatalysts that exploit peroxide-bridge intermediates
for selective C‒H bond activation.
iv) The Met–π interaction network controls pathway bifurcation and offers a new
engineering principle. The structure of OkaE in complex with okaramine A
reveals a unique the Met–π interaction network (M64-M71-W79-M122) that envelops
the A-ring of the substrate. Site-directed mutagenesis demonstrates that this
network is critical structural determinant of reaction bifurcation: the M71A variant
shifts selectivity toward the H8a–HAT pathway, yielding predominantly 6,
whereas W79A disrupts bifurcation entirely. This provides decisive experimental
evidence that Met–π network is not merely structural but functionally essential.
Furthermore, this study offers the first example of leveraging a Met–π interaction
network to engineer catalytic pathway bifurcation for natural product
diversification.
v) A distal αKG-binding mode enables novel oxygen activation. The OkaE enzyme
and substrate complex exhibits a distal-type αKG-binding mode that prevents
conventional rebound hydroxylation. QM/MM calculations support a feasible
azetidine-formation pathway and reveal that rotation of the FeIV=O species initiates
two competing HAT channels (3a-OH–HAT and H8a–HAT), rationalizing the
product diversity. This study expands the repertoire of distal-type αKG enzymes
and provides quantitative computational validation of their potential for non-
canonical oxygen activation mechanisms, offering new prospects for predicting
and engineering novel enzyme functions.
(2) Regarding structural interpretations issue on “…the work is not thorough: the
mechanistic evidence is insufficiently supported; the structural interpretations are
speculative…”:
In response, we have conducted additional experiments that substantially
strengthen the support for our proposed mechanism. While we believe our original
structural interpretations remain well-founded, the newly acquired data enhanced
mechanistic validation:
i) The electron density for the substrate and the coordinating residues is clear and
unambiguous. A mFo-DFc maps have been provided in the SI document (Figures
S18 and S21).
16
ii) The proposed roles of active site residues are directly inferred from the observed
hydrogen-bonding and electrostatic interactions in the structure. The A–E rings of 1
adopt a catalytically competent conformation in the binding pocket formed by M64,
M71, W79, N118, M122, L227, and T273. Especially, a unique Met–π interaction
network involving residues M64-M71-W79-M122 envelops the A-ring of 1, orientating
active sites C8aand O3a toward the active centre. Furthermore, these proposed roles
are consistent with and supported by the outcomes of our alanine scanning
mutagenesis of residues M64, M71, W79, and M122.
iii) As detailed in our response to Comment #4, QM/MM calculations support the
assignment that 3, 4, 5, and 6 are generated through H8a–HAT pathway, whereas 7
is formed via 3a-OH–HAT, thereby providing a theoretical basis for the observed
product divergence.
iv) Following the reviewer’s suggestion, mixed 16O /18O labeling experiments were
2 2
performed. The resulting isotopic distribution supports the involvement of a second
O molecule in the formation of 7, as further elaborated in our response to Comment
2
#7.
In summary, we believe the revised manuscript presents a comprehensive and
novel mechanistic study of OkaE. The combination of in vitro biochemistry, structural
biology, and computational modeling provides a compelling and multi-faceted
mechanism. We have thoroughly revised the text to better highlight the novelty and
mechanistic insights of our work and are confident that the manuscript in its current
form meets the standards for publication. We sincerely thank the reviewer’s valuable
suggestions, which have significantly improved the quality and clarity of our
manuscript.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript reports the structural and mechanistic insights into the α-ketoglutarate (αKG)-dependent non-heme iron
enzyme OkaE that builds the azetidine ring in okaramine biosynthesis. In vitro reconstitution of OkaE with okaramine A (1)
produced okaramine E (3), 12-dehydroxy-okaramine E (2), and four new congeners, neokaramines I–IV (4–7). Crystal
structures of OkaE•Co²⁺, OkaE•Co²⁺•αKG, and OkaE•Co²⁺•αKG•okaramine A revealed a homodimeric double-stranded β-
helix fold, a distal-type αKG binding mode, and placement of substrate atoms C8a and O3a near the metal center within a
pocket framed by M64, M71, M122, and W79. QM/MM calculations supported the distal αKG geometry and showed substrate
positioning that shortens Op–H8a and Op–H3a distances (≈4.8→2.9 Å and 5.1→2.6 Å). Site-directed mutagenesis indicated
that M71A biases H8a hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT), W79A reduces overall reactivity, and M122A modestly enhances
formation of 7 via O3a-HAT; structures of M64A, M71A, and W79A complexes corroborate these product profiles. Isotope-
18O-labeling showed mixed O₂/H₂O incorporation into 3–6, consistent with hydroxyl-rebound and/or cationic pathways,
whereas 7 incorporates only O₂, implying rare capture of a second O₂ within a single catalytic cycle. Together, the data
support a mechanism in which H8a-HAT drives azetidine formation followed by sequential

### Reviewer 3

“Structural and Mechanistic Insights into Azetidine-associated αKG NHFe Enzyme OkaE with Multifunctional Catalysis” by
Wang, Yu, Liu, Zhang, Zhu, Yan, and Liu et al. is about OkaE, a α-Ketoglutarate-dependent mononuclear non-haem iron
enzyme that can synthesize a pharmacophoric motif azetidine ring via unique C–C bond formation. The authors find that
OkaE also performs sequential oxidations such as hydroxylations, epoxidation, and ring cleavages. The authors find that not
one but two oxygen molecules are involved for sequential epoxidation and ring cleavage. The authors use a host of
experimental techniques (isotopic labeling, X-ray crystallography, and protein engineering), along with QM/MM calculations
to understand the reactivity of OkaE.
Although this article is well written and sound, I have a few concerns that should be addressed prior to publication of the
article. I commend the authors on a comprehensive work with the methods being described in a very reproducible way. I
urge the authors to consider my suggestions below and upload their simulation data so that it can be reused by the
community..
1. The authors mention that OkaE undergoes HAT. Are the authors sure about this, or do they mean Proton-Coupled
Electron Transfer (PCET) in the general sense? https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/anie.201805511. Here, HAT
may imply a mechanistic picture that the authors are not fully implying. There should be a clarification on this point.
2. How did the authors choose their E-value threshold for the sequence similarity analysis? Is this just a strict cutoff that finds
the most similar sequences? If so, why not a multiple sequence alignment?
3. The authors mention that the substrate binding pocket size is reduced by 10% when they analyze their structures. Is this a
fair analysis? Static structures may not indicate the true reduction in the effective pocket size which may be influenced by the
dynamics. Is the spread of this pocket size minimal? The authors may have an answer from their QM/MM simulations.
4. There are some typos that should be fixed. Page 12 line 227, “coplaner”. Page 18 line 329: ‘to addressing this’
5. In figure 4b, why do the bars not all add up to 100%? At a minimum, shouldn’t the wild type bars add up to 100%?
6. The isotope labeling experiments in this work are beautiful. However, I do not follow why the alphaKG ratio being altered
to 4:1 indicates the involvement of the second dioxygen. This should be explained in a bit more detail for readers. The
speciation of the second oxygen must be different if it is what the readers indicate. What is the form of this hypothesized
second oxygen species likely to be?
7. When altering between axial and equatorial conformations for the iron oxo, there may be a transition state:
https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acscatal.2c01143. How would OkaE overcome such a barrier in the proposed
mechanism? Some commentary on this would be helpful.
8. I urge the authors to upload their data to zenodo instead of making their data available upon request. This will facilitate the
reuse of the authors’ work.
The article is well written. Thus, I’d like to commend the authors on this effort.

relationships of OkaE and demonstrates its potential to be reprogrammed to tailor and

Response:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We have carefully
considered the critiques regarding the novelty and thoroughness of our study. While we
acknowledge that the αKG-dependent non-haem iron enzyme family is known for its
catalytic versatility, we believe our work on OkaE provides several new insights that
substantially advance the field. Below, we address the specific concerns point by point,
and we hope the reviewer will find our response and the additional clarifications in the
revised manuscript persuasive.
(1) Regarding novelty issue on “…the study lacks novelty since the catalytic
versatility of this enzyme family is well documented, and the presented findings do
not substantially advance mechanistic understanding…”:
We apologize for the insufficient emphasis on these aspects in the original
manuscript. Our study on OkaE presents several key advances, as summarized below:
i) OkaE represents a new paradigm in enzymatic scaffold diversification. Unlike
previously reported systems by Lin group3, OkaE enzyme is a single enzyme
capable that catalyzes multiple distinct chemical steps, including hydroxylation,
cyclization, and possibly rearrangement, to assemble and diversify a complex
azetidine-containing scaffold. This function versatility provides a new biosynthetic
model for scaffold diversification in natural product biosynthesis.
ii) First atomic-resolution view of azetidine formation. By integrating of
crystallography with QM/MM simulations, we provide the first atomic-level
insight into azetidine ring formation within this enzyme family, addressing a novel
and unresolved mechanistic question.
iii) Discovery of a potential new peroxygenase-like activity in non-heme iron
enzyme. Our isotopic labeling experiments reveal that OkaE incorporates an
oxygen molecule to form an endoperoxide during catalysis. This function trait,
observed in only a few αKG-dependent non-haem iron enzyme such as FtmOx17-
15
11and NvfI12, suggests that OkaE may represent a third functionally distinct system
capable of endoperoxide formation. This finding not only expands the mechanistic
repertoire of this enzyme family but also highlights OkaE as a promising starting
point for engineering novel biocatalysts that exploit peroxide-bridge intermediates
for selective C‒H bond activation.
iv) The Met–π interaction network controls pathway bifurcation and offers a new
engineering principle. The structure of OkaE in complex with okaramine A
reveals a unique the Met–π interaction network (M64-M71-W79-M122) that envelops
the A-ring of the substrate. Site-directed mutagenesis demonstrates that this
network is critical structural determinant of reaction bifurcation: the M71A variant
shifts selectivity toward the H8a–HAT pathway, yielding predominantly 6,
whereas W79A disrupts bifurcation entirely. This provides decisive experimental
evidence that Met–π network is not merely structural but functionally essential.
Furthermore, this study offers the first example of leveraging a Met–π interaction
network to engineer catalytic pathway bifurcation for natural product
diversification.
v) A distal αKG-binding mode enables novel oxygen activation. The OkaE enzyme
and substrate complex exhibits a distal-type αKG-binding mode that prevents
conventional rebound hydroxylation. QM/MM calculations support a feasible
azetidine-formation pathway and reveal that rotation of the FeIV=O species initiates
two competing HAT channels (3a-OH–HAT and H8a–HAT), rationalizing the
product diversity. This study expands the repertoire of distal-type αKG enzymes
and provides quantitative computational validation of their potential for non-
canonical oxygen activation mechanisms, offering new prospects for predicting
and engineering novel enzyme functions.

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. OkaE follows the classical

3. How did the authors choose their E-value threshold for the sequence similarity
analysis? Is this just a strict cutoff that finds the most similar sequences? If so, why not
a multiple sequence alignment?
Response:
The E-value threshold was chosen based on established practice in BLAST-based
sequence similarity searches, where increasingly stringent cutoffs are commonly
applied to balance sensitivity and specificity. Specifically, we examined three
thresholds (10−30, 10−50, and 10−70) to ensure that our results were not dependent on a
single value. This approach allowed us to focus on highly similar sequences, thereby
enabling reliable structural comparison and mechanistic interpretation. While multiple
sequence alignment is indeed a powerful complementary method, its primary utility lies
in identifying conserved motifs and residue-level variation across a broader set of
homologs. Our specific aim here was instead to capture the most closely related
homologous sequences to guide structural modeling and functional inference. For this
purpose, E-value–based filtering provides a more direct and appropriate framework.

30

direct the oxo group into the equatorial position during the formation of Int1a, thereby
avoiding the need for a subsequent axial-to-equatorial transition.
